basis: Static reverse engineering of original bytes; no specimen executed.
method: Read RULES.md and TAXONOMY.md before authoring.
Run atomscan and cleave facts for each supplied file; preserve raw output under scratch/triage-bad.
Trace native entry points, network dispatch, file writes, activation and restoration with Rizin.
Decode the subtract/XOR controller and strided complemented strings manually.
Check all emitted hostile/suspicious findings and compare all original trait IDs, including the embedded PE.
Use CLEAVE_VALIDATE=0 only during scans: installed Atomscan preflight rejects an already documented 101-rule naming budget. Final validation uses the current source-matched Cleave release binary.

samples.identification: Native Winlogon DDoS/download bot posing as Get MAC Address
samples.verdict_reason: Remote binary tasking, downloaded executable activation, sustained datagram bursts and an extra Winlogon Userinit command contradict the claimed MAC-address utility purpose.
traces: 0x402120 copies itself to Windows/Tasks/conime.exe, launches the copy hidden and deletes the previous image.
0x401f80 concatenates the normal system Userinit program, a comma and the installed image, then calls the resolved registry writer on HKLM Winlogon/Userinit.
0x401dd0 transforms each controller byte as ((byte-44) & 255) XOR 44. The resulting endpoint is www.asis0day.biz:8095; 0x4015f0 parses it and connects.
0x401910 receives an eight-byte header, uses its first dword as the body length and its second dword for task dispatch. The helper at 0x4017d0 reads through recv.
0x401c58 resolves URLDownloadToFileA, downloads the URL from the received record and passes the same output pathname to WinExec.
0x402a40 sends eighteen datagrams per burst, sleeps 20 ms and repeats until the global stop flag changes.
samples.changes: Add bound socket-task/payload, Winlogon and datagram-flood detections plus neutral download-to-execution, flood-loop and subtract/XOR observations.
samples.missing_context: No live host deployment or controller reachability was observed; family names in the collection filename are not attribution evidence.
samples.marker_line: Winlogon DDoS bot: remote payload execution and login persistence

samples.identification: Self-variant upload wrapper carrying a native module-command implant
samples.verdict_reason: The carried implant accepts executable modules, invokes their entry exports and establishes an automatic service. These attack capabilities and concealed configuration tip the verdict despite the outer uploader potentially serving a test harness.
traces: Outer entry reaches 0x4013a0. It reads its own complete image, locates a ten-byte marker, rewrites the following sixteen bytes with PRNG output, writes a randomly named executable, uploads it and deletes the temporary file in a repeating loop.

The upload uses libcurl multipart fields file[], node and submit. The URL is http://wecan.hasthe.technology/upload; node is NODE1 through NODE7. There is no local launch of the generated variants in this wrapper.
A complete PE starts at file offset 0x3b000. Its SHA256 is 2dcb71be18a4b7aec90d3efa8b980b161261d7b5c36f32a071e12b940721c24f.
Embedded 0x403350 complements low bytes at a stride of two, recovering DLL upload/load status and other command strings.
Embedded 0x4027e0 branches on received-record byte six: 0x88 uploads/loads a DLL, while 0x89 stages an EXE replacement.
Embedded 0x402550 calls LoadLibraryA and resolves/invokes Load, Run, Stop and Unload exports.
Embedded 0x4043f0 calls CreateServiceA with service type 0x110 and start type 2, then starts the service.
samples.changes: No changes to the existing two hostile implant findings or the supported strided-string obfuscation detection.
samples.missing_context: No uploader-server behavior or operator authorization was supplied. The wrapper may be a deployment/test harness; the complete embedded command implant still supports MALICIOUS. Collection labels such as ransomware/stealer do not establish those behaviors.
samples.marker_line: Native module implant: remote DLL execution and auto-start service

samples.identification: DG.386 DOS COM infector memory image
samples.verdict_reason: Enumerates and opens other COM files, saves their original entry bytes, overwrites the entry with a relative jump and appends its own 386-byte body.
traces: The 647-byte file has a 256-byte zero prefix; code begins at file offset 0x100. Treat it as a memory-image representation, not proof of a directly runnable normal COM file.
0x128 and 0x143 issue DOS find-first/find-next using *.com. 0x15b opens the default DTA filename at 0x9e for read/write.
0x168 obtains EOF and saves the original host length. It checks bytes near the old EOF as a reinfection marker.
0x1b9 reads three original entry bytes. 0x1d7 writes a three-byte E9 header whose displacement is host length minus three.
0x1f2 seeks to EOF; 0x200 writes its own code from 0x105 for 0x182 bytes (386).
0x237 restores the saved three-byte entry at memory 0x100 and jumps there after restoring the DTA state.
samples.changes: Add a bound append/entry observation to the existing COM append-and-entry infection composite and a neutral entry-copy/handback observation. Correct the false far-call matcher.
samples.coverage_gap: Only one distinct hostile outcome is supported: parasitic COM infection. Enumeration, entry patching, replication and host restoration are parts of that outcome. No second hostile objective is established; no duplicate rules were added to reach a count.
samples.missing_context: This is a serialized old DOS virus image. Runtime success on a present-day machine was not tested and is not required to identify its hostile code.
samples.classifier_gap: Installed Atomscan 2.13.0 treats this original file as unknown and emits no traits. Current Cleave identifies dos_com and emits the new hostile infection finding. The legacy ML result remains unflagged.
samples.marker_line: DG DOS virus image: COM entry hijack and self-appending infection
